# Substrate Dossier — "How SQLite became the most-deployed database on earth"

## 1. One-line spine
One engineer wrote a tiny SQL engine for a US Navy warship, gave it away to the public domain, and three choices — serverless, single-file, give-it-away — turned it into the silent default inside every phone, browser, and plane on earth.

## 2. The origin (dated)

- **Creator.** SQLite was created by **D. Richard Hipp** (full name Dwayne Richard Hipp; goes by "D. Richard Hipp" / "Richard Hipp"), its sole original author and still its project lead. *(sqlite.org/about.html, Wikipedia, CoRecursive)*
- **When work began.** Hipp **designed SQLite in the spring of 2000** (sqlite.org/about dates the project start to **2000-05-09**); in the CoRecursive interview he dates the genesis to "back in 2000." *(sqlite.org/about.html, Wikipedia, CoRecursive)*
- **The Navy context.** He built it in 2000 **while contracting for Bath Iron Works** (a General Dynamics shipbuilding subsidiary since 1995) **on software for the US Navy guided-missile destroyer USS Oscar Austin, hull DDG-79.** Wikipedia frames the employer as "General Dynamics on contract with the United States Navy"; both framings are the same job. **DDG-79 is an Arleigh Burke-class (Flight IIA) guided-missile destroyer, commissioned 19 August 2000 at Norfolk, Virginia** — *not* a battleship (the CoRecursive host loosely says "battleship"; do not repeat that). *(CoRecursive, Wikipedia: SQLite / USS Oscar Austin / Bath Iron Works)*
- **The ship application.** A damage-control program ("Automated Common Diagrams") that told sailors which valves to open/close to isolate battle damage; pipe-routing and valve-location data lived in an on-ship database. *(CoRecursive)*
- **The why.** The ship's preinstalled client/server database (Informix) would intermittently go down and take Hipp's application with it ("Cannot connect to database server"). His insight: the app only needed to read data into RAM — *"Why do we even need a server? Why can't I pull this directly off the disk drive?"* A colleague said, "Richard, why don't you just write one?" The independent VLDB paper frames SQLite as "born out of the frustration of debugging a database server running in a separate process." *(CoRecursive, VLDB p3535-gaffney.pdf)*
- **The naming.** "SQLite" plays on "light." Hipp: *"I say S-Q-L-ite, like a mineral"* (confirmed verbatim, plus his own X post); indifferent to "sequel-lite" / "SQL-lite." *(Changelog #201, Wikipedia)*
- **The public-domain choice.** Hipp wanted "a much more liberal license so people could just toss this into their application and not have to worry about it," choosing public domain over BSD/MIT. *(Changelog #201, copyright.html)*

**Version milestones (all dates verbatim from sqlite.org chronology / release logs):**
- **1.0 — 2000-08-17** (first release; 1.0.1 the next day, 2000-08-18). Note the documentary coincidence: SQLite 1.0 shipped **two days before** USS Oscar Austin was commissioned (19 Aug 2000). Built on the **gdbm** (GNU Database Manager) key/value backend (used 1.0–1.0.32). *(chronology.html, Wikipedia)*
- **2.0.0 — 2001-09-28** — replaced gdbm with **Hipp's own custom B-tree** storage engine (used 2.0.0–2.8.17). Hipp notes 2.0 "came out just a couple days after the 9/11 event" (his loose phrasing; actually ~17 days). *(chronology.html, versionnumbers.html, Changelog #201)*
- **3.0.0 — 2004-06-18** — from-scratch new B+tree file format (databases "25% to 35% smaller" than 2.8), UTF-8/UTF-16 internationalization, manifest typing, BLOB support, 64-bit ROWIDs, user-defined collations; the "sqlite3" file/API naming dates from here. (Was labeled an alpha at release.) *(chronology.html, version3.html, releaselog/3_0_0.html)*
- **3.7.0 — 2010-07-21** — introduced **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**. *(releaselog/3_7_0.html, wal.html)*

## 3. Why it won — the architecture

SQLite's self-definition (verbatim, About page): **"an in-process library that implements a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine."** Those four adjectives are the embeddability thesis. *(about.html)*

1. **Serverless / in-process.** *"With SQLite, the process that wants to access the database reads and writes directly from the database files on disk. There is no intermediary server process."* Where Postgres/MySQL/Oracle require a separate server process reached over a socket, SQLite is linked into the application and reads the file in-process — the direct answer to the failing-Informix-server origin problem. *(different.html)*
2. **Single file.** *"A complete SQL database with multiple tables, indices, triggers, and views, is contained in a single disk file."* The entire database — schema plus data — is one ordinary cross-platform file you can copy, email, or move. Every valid file begins with the 16-byte UTF-8 string **"SQLite format 3\000"** (hex `53 51 4c 69 74 65 20 66 6f 72 6d 61 74 20 33 00`); pages are a power of two between 512 and 65536 bytes; max database ~281 TB. The format **"is used by all releases of SQLite since version 3.0.0 (2004-06-18)"** — databases written ~20 years ago still open today. *(about.html, different.html, fileformat2.html)*
3. **Zero-configuration.** *"SQLite does not need to be 'installed' before it is used. There is no 'setup' procedure... SQLite just works."* No daemon, no config file, no DBA, no administrator account. *(different.html)*
4. **The positioning — exact wording:** **"SQLite does not compete with client/server databases. SQLite competes with fopen()."** (On whentouse.html, in the intro before the numbered headings; "fopen()" with parentheses, two sentences. NOT on appfileformat.html.) The rationale, also verbatim: SQLite "is not directly comparable to client/server SQL database engines such as MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server since SQLite is trying to solve a different problem" — those engines "emphasize scalability, concurrency, centralization, and control," while "SQLite emphasizes economy, efficiency, reliability, independence, and simplicity." Hipp's spoken version (Changelog #201): *"We don't compete against Oracle, we compete against fopen."* *(whentouse.html, Changelog #201)*
5. **The amalgamation (the practical drop-in).** SQLite ships as one large C file, **sqlite3.c**, combining over 100 source files into a single translation unit — **238K lines (145K excluding blanks/comments), over 8.4 MB, as of 2021-12-29** (111 core C files + 22 extension files as of v3.37.0). You add two files (sqlite3.c + sqlite3.h) to your build. Compiling as one translation unit also yields machine code **"between 5% and 10% faster"** via better inter-procedure/inlining optimization (measured, compiler-dependent). *(amalgamation.html)*
6. **Tiny.** With all features enabled the library **"can be less than 900KiB"** depending on platform/compiler; the Distinctive Features page says the whole library is **"less than 1MiB."** (Use <900KiB / <1MiB — do NOT cite an older "<750KiB" whole-library figure.) *(about.html, different.html, footprint.html)*
7. **Portability via the VFS.** The Virtual File System (OS Interface) "is what makes SQLite portable across operating systems" — the bottom module that every other module calls when it needs the OS (open/read/write/close a file, current time, randomness). Pluggable: a new VFS subclasses three objects (sqlite3_vfs, sqlite3_file, sqlite3_io_methods) and registers via sqlite3_vfs_register(). *(vfs.html, arch.html)*
8. **The stack & bytecode VM.** Interface (C API) → Tokenizer → Parser (Lemon-generated from parse.y) → Code Generator → **Virtual Machine / bytecode engine (vdbe.c)** → B-tree (btree.c) → Pager / Page Cache (pager.c, wal.c, pcache.c) → VFS. SQL is compiled to bytecode run on a register-based VDBE. "Separate B-trees are used for each table and each index... All B-trees are stored in the same disk file." *(arch.html)*
9. **Manifest (dynamic) typing.** *"In SQLite, the datatype of a value is associated with the value itself, not with its container"* — unlike "every SQL database engine other than SQLite," which ties type to the column. Five storage classes: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB. (Heritage: SQLite "started life as a Tcl extension that escaped into the wild" — Tcl's flexible typing is the origin of manifest typing; the test suite is still written in Tcl.) *(datatype3.html, different.html, famous.html, Changelog #201)*
10. **Concurrency — rollback journal vs WAL.**
    - *Rollback journal (default):* before changing a page, the original page is copied to a separate `-journal` file; changes go into the main DB; **deleting the journal is the atomic commit.** A crash leaves a "hot journal" that the next process rolls back.
    - *WAL (since 3.7.0):* inverts this — original pages stay in the main DB, new pages are appended to a `-wal` file (plus a `-shm` shared-memory index); commit is a record appended to the WAL. Verbatim: *"Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time. However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time."* WAL did **not** give SQLite multiple concurrent writers — the single-writer ceiling remains.
    - *Locking model (rollback mode):* whole-file granularity, five states (UNLOCKED, SHARED, RESERVED, PENDING, EXCLUSIVE). "Any number of processes can hold SHARED locks at the same time... But no other thread or process is allowed to write... while one or more SHARED locks are active." *(lockingv3.html, wal.html)*

## 4. The reliability legend

- **Test-to-code ratio (exact, with as-of date).** *"As of version 3.42.0 (2023-05-16), the SQLite library consists of approximately 155.8 KSLOC of C code. By comparison, the project has 590 times as much test code and test scripts — 92053.1 KSLOC."* The live page still cites 3.42.0 for this stat. *(testing.html)*
- **Coverage.** The proprietary **TH3** harness achieves **100% branch coverage and 100% MC/DC (Modified Condition/Decision Coverage)** over the core library; 100% MC/DC was first reached **2009-07-25** (first code laid down 2008-09-25 — ~10 months). TH3 is ~1055.4 KSLOC implementing 50,362 distinct test cases; a full-coverage run is ~2.4 million test instances. *(th3.html, testing.html)*
- **FOUR independent harnesses** (see corrections — *not three*): TCL tests (open-source, ship with SQLite — 27.2 KSLOC, 1390 files, 51,445 cases), **TH3** (proprietary, 100% MC/DC), **SQL Logic Test** (7.2 million queries / 1.12 GB, cross-checked against PostgreSQL, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle 10g), and **dbsqlfuzz** (proprietary fuzzer, mutates SQL text *and* the DB file, ~**1 billion test mutations per day** on ~16 cores). *(testing.html)*
- **Aviation angle.** TH3 was designed "to support the rigorous testing standards of **DO-178B**" after avionics manufacturers expressed interest in SQLite (DO-178B's hallmark is 100% MC/DC). Hipp's on-record human origin (CoRecursive): *"I'd been doing some work for Rockwell Collins, an avionics manufacturer... they introduced me to this concept of DO-178B,"* and bringing SQLite to 100% MC/DC *"took a year of 60 hour weeks."* *(th3.html, CoRecursive)*

## 5. The ubiquity payoff (the title's promise — be precise)

These are **SQLite's own self-published, explicitly hedged estimates**, not independently audited counts. State them as the project's estimate.

- **Headline (verbatim, famous.html):** *"SQLite is the most widely deployed database engine in the world today."* Companion page mostdeployed.html is titled "Most Widely Deployed and Used Database Engine."
- **The trillion (verbatim, mostdeployed.html, page updated 2026-04-21):** *"Since SQLite is used extensively in every smartphone, and there are more than 4.0 billion (4.0e9) smartphones in active use, each holding hundreds of SQLite database files, it seems likely that there are over one trillion (1e12) SQLite databases in active use."* (Counts database *files*, not library copies. The 4.0B-smartphone input is conservative vs. ~7.4B active devices today, so the floor holds.)
- **Stronger framing (verbatim):** *"SQLite is likely used more than all other database engines combined."* Present as SQLite's own estimate — softer/less verifiable than "most widely deployed." Do not pair the two as if equally proven.
- **Library ranking (verbatim "best guess"):** *"the second mostly widely deployed software library, after libz"* — but the same page hedges that SQLite "might be the single most widely deployed and used software component" (static linking ⇒ many instances per device), and "probably one of the top five most deployed software modules of any description." Independent experts (curl/zlib author Daniel Stenberg) say zlib/SQLite/libcurl can't be reliably ranked. **Present "second after zlib" as a self-hedged guess, not fact.**
- **Hipp's human-voice version:** per Craig Stuntz's notes of Hipp's **10 October 2017** talk, Hipp "thinks there are more than one trillion SQLite databases in use" and there are "more copies of the library than there are people on earth." (These are Stuntz's paraphrased live-tweets, not a verbatim transcript; 2020-11-30 is only the blog publish date.) "Billions and billions of copies of SQLite exist in the wild" is verbatim on mostdeployed.html. *(craigstuntz.com, mostdeployed.html)*
- **Where it ships (verbatim list, mostdeployed.html):** Every Android device, every iPhone/iOS device, every Mac, every Windows 10/11 installation, and every Firefox, Chrome, and Safari browser. PHP and Python ship it built in (every Python distribution since Python 2.5). *(mostdeployed.html, famous.html)*
- **Named users (famous.html):** Airbus (A350 XWB flight software), Apple, Google (Android + Chrome), Adobe (Photoshop Lightroom file format), Dropbox (client-side primary data store), Mozilla (Firefox/Thunderbird), Bosch (GM/Nissan/Suzuki automotive multimedia), Facebook (osquery query engine), Microsoft (core component of Windows 10), plus iTunes, Skype, TurboTax/QuickBooks. *(famous.html)* — *Note the hedging in §8.*
- **The airplane fact (verbatim, famous.html):** *"Airbus confirms that SQLite is being used in the flight software for the A350 XWB family of aircraft."* — **See §8 correction: do NOT claim this is safety-critical DO-178B flight-control software.**
- **The Library of Congress fact:** *"SQLite is a Recommended Storage Format for datasets according to the US Library of Congress"* (locrsf.html, dated **2018-05-29**). The LoC's own format ID is **FDD000461 ("SQLite, Version 3")**; SQLite remains listed in the 2024–2025 / 2025–2026 RFS editions. Why it qualifies: a stable, fully-documented, public-domain open file format. — *See §8 on the "only XML/JSON/CSV" detail.*
- **Bonus archival fact:** the developers' "35% Faster Than The Filesystem" benchmark — SQLite reads/writes small blobs ~35% faster than equivalent individual files, with ~20% less disk space (their own test, 100,000 random 8–12 KB blobs; "the 35% figure is approximate"). *(fasterthanfs.html)*

## 6. The paradox (no company, yet everywhere)

- **Public domain, not open-source license.** *"All of the code and documentation in SQLite has been dedicated to the public domain by the authors."* / *"No claim of copyright is made on any part of the core source code."* Anyone may "copy, modify, publish, use, compile, sell, or distribute" it for any purpose. It's a *dedication*, not a license — there's no copyright to license. *(copyright.html, different.html)*
- **Closed to contributions, by design.** From the README: *"Because SQLite is in the public domain, we do not normally accept pull requests, because if we did take a pull request, the changes in that pull request might carry a copyright and the SQLite source code would then no longer be fully in the public domain."* Contributors who do submit code sign **affidavits dedicating their work to the public domain** — originals stored in a **firesafe at Hwaci's offices**. The model: "open source but not open contribution." *(copyright.html, README, whynotgit.html)*
- **Fossil, not Git/GitHub.** The canonical source lives in a **Fossil repository** (Hipp's own version-control system, built specifically for SQLite, with no pull-request interface). *"If you are reading this on GitHub... then you are looking at a mirror. The Fossil repository contains the urtext."* *(README, whynotgit.html)*
- **The company.** **Hwaci (Hipp, Wyrick & Company, Inc.)**, a small North Carolina S-corporation founded **1992**, owned by the husband-and-wife team **Richard Hipp and Ginger Wyrick**; it employs all SQLite developers. *(hwaci.com, copyright.html)*
- **How it earns money (the give-it-away-yet-sustainable engine):**
  - **SQLite Consortium** — membership fee **$120,000/year** (canonical member page; the prosupport summary's $150K is stale — use $120K). Members get the developers' undivided attention **23 staff-days/year** plus 24/7 phone access. Launched **December 12, 2007**, charter members **Mozilla and Symbian Ltd.** Purpose: keep SQLite "independent and fully under the control of the SQLite developers." *(com/member.html, consortium.html, pressrelease-20071212.html)*
  - **SQLite Encryption Extension (SEE)** — perpetual source license, one-time **US $2,000**. *(com/see.html)*
  - **Warranty of Title** — a legal document Hwaci sells to organizations whose lawyers need the public-domain claim to be defensible (and for jurisdictions that don't recognize the public domain). Proceeds fund SQLite. *(copyright.html, purchase/license)*
  - **Paid support** — Annual Maintenance Subscription **$1,500/year**; Technical Support Agreement generally **$8,000–$35,000/year** (up to $85,000). *(prosupport.html — flagged medium confidence; public pages route through a quote form.)*
- **Longevity pledge.** *"The intent of the developers is to support SQLite through the year 2050,"* with a promise "to keep the SQLite C-language API and on-disk format fully backwards compatible" (lts.html — Airbus is NOT cited as the reason here). Hwaci separately commits to "continue operating in its current form, and at roughly its current size until at least the year 2050." *(lts.html, prosupport.html)*

## 7. The forward look

- **SQLite officially in the browser (WASM).** The sqlite3 WASM/JS subproject is *"the first effort 'officially' associated with the SQLite project."* SQLite **3.40.0, released 2022-11-16**, was the first release to ship the JS/WASM components; sqlite.org/wasm went online October 2022. (Earlier community builds: Alon Zakai's sql.js, "the first known direct usage of sqlite3 in a web browser, dating back to 2012.") *(wasm/about.md, devclass.com)*
- **OPFS persistence.** The Origin-Private FileSystem is *"an API providing browser-side persistent storage which... sqlite3 can use for storing databases"* — what makes an in-browser SQLite DB survive a reload. Supported in Chromium (mid-2022+), Firefox 111+, Safari 16.4+; the high-concurrency OPFS VFS needs COOP/COEP headers (SharedArrayBuffer). Google's Chrome team frames official SQLite-Wasm + OPFS as the successor to the deprecated Web SQL: *"The SQLite Wasm library with the Origin Private File System persistence backend is our fulfillment of this promise."* *(wasm/persistence.md, developer.chrome.com)*
- **libSQL / Turso.** **libSQL** is *"an open source, open contribution fork of SQLite, created and maintained by Turso,"* announced **October 2022**, MIT-licensed — explicitly contrasting SQLite's closed-contribution model. Adds embedded replicas, a server for remote access, ALTER TABLE column-type changes, WASM user-defined functions, a virtual WAL interface. On **2025-01-21**, Turso announced it is **rewriting SQLite from scratch in Rust** (codenamed "Limbo," now "Turso"), async-first (io_uring-ready), maintaining "full compatibility with SQLite at both file and language levels." **Flag as in-progress beta, not a shipped replacement;** libSQL (fork) and the Turso rewrite are distinct projects. *(github tursodatabase/libsql, turso.tech blogs)*
- **Cloudflare D1.** *"Cloudflare's managed, serverless database with SQLite's SQL semantics,"* GA **2024-04-01**, 10 GB databases, 50,000 databases/account, plus Time Travel (restore to any minute in the last 30 days) and global read replication. *(blog.cloudflare.com, developers.cloudflare.com/d1)*
- **Litestream & LiteFS.** **Litestream** (Ben Johnson) runs as a separate process to *"continuously stream SQLite changes to your preferred cloud storage or local files"* with "no code changes" — disaster-recovery/point-in-time replication to object storage. **LiteFS** (Fly.io) is *"a distributed file system that transparently replicates SQLite databases"* across cluster nodes (FUSE-based, leader/replica with a lease) — "right next to your application on the edge." Flag LiteFS as production-but-cautioned (pre-1.0; Fly.io warns against combining with Machines autostop/autostart — stale-lease rollback risk). *(litestream.io, fly.io/docs/litefs)*
- **Local-first framing.** The 2019 Ink & Switch essay *"Local-first software: you own your data, in spite of the cloud"* (Martin Kleppmann et al.) defines the movement via seven ideals and positions CRDTs as foundational. Treat as a movement/trend, not a metric. *(inkandswitch.com)*
- **SQLite-as-application-file-format.** *"An SQLite database file with a defined schema often makes an excellent application file format"* — proposed as a fourth category alongside custom formats, pile-of-files, and wrapped pile-of-files (real examples: Adobe Lightroom, Bentley Microstation). *(appfileformat.html)*

## 8. Confidence & corrections — what NOT to assert

- **"Battleship" — WRONG. Do not use.** USS Oscar Austin (DDG-79) is a **guided-missile destroyer**, not a battleship. The CoRecursive host says "battleship" loosely; the correct term is destroyer. *(Confirmed by multiple Navy/Wikipedia sources.)*
- **Airbus A350 — do NOT claim safety-critical flight controls.** The verbatim famous.html quote ("flight software for the A350 XWB family") is accurate, but on record Hipp says he does **not** believe SQLite is used in safety-critical A350 applications — it **logs maintenance activities** so ground crews get a printout of what needs fixing on landing. "Flight software" covers non-safety-critical onboard systems. **The direct causal tie "SQLite's 100% MC/DC testing exists because of the A350" is an overstatement** — the MC/DC effort originated with Hipp's earlier Rockwell Collins work and predates/ is independent of the Airbus relationship. Also: "Airbus confirms" is SQLite's own attribution; there is no independent Airbus press statement.
- **"Three test harnesses" — STALE. Say FOUR** (TCL, TH3, SQL Logic Test, dbsqlfuzz). The current testing.html lists four.
- **"Second-most-deployed library after zlib" — SELF-HEDGED GUESS, not fact.** SQLite's own page says it might be #1; independent experts say the ranking is impossible. Always attribute to "SQLite's own best guess."
- **The trillion / "most deployed" / "more than all other engines combined" — SQLite's OWN estimates,** explicitly hedged ("seems likely," "best guess"). Never present as an audited census. Note the page's own heading qualifies it as the most-deployed *SQL database engine*.
- **Library of Congress "only XML, JSON, and CSV" — sqlite.org's own 2018 simplification.** The actual 2018 LoC list also named **TSV and fixed-width**. Keep the "**as of 2018-05-29**" date qualifier and attribute the three-format phrasing to sqlite.org's page, not to the LoC verbatim. The "supported through 2050" number does NOT appear on locrsf.html (it's a separate lts.html pledge) — keep them distinct.
- **2.0.0 "Berkeley DB sold to Oracle" rationale** comes from the **CoRecursive** interview, NOT The Changelog (on Changelog his reason was that Berkeley DB's documentation was too vague). "Adding transactions" in 2.0 is secondary/consensus (Wikipedia), not stated on sqlite.org's own version pages — soften to "commonly attributed."
- **Named users — several are hedged on famous.html itself:** Dropbox is "reported to use" SQLite as primary client-side store; Skype rests on "multiple sightings"; Intuit (QuickBooks/TurboTax) is inferred "apparently... from error reports." The flat "Every instance of..." phrasing comes from mostdeployed.html. Names are correct; don't overstate vendor confirmation.
- **Folklore / cut-or-flag (do NOT state as primary fact):**
  - **iMessage/WhatsApp "stored in SQLite"** — journalist framing from the CoRecursive host's intro, **not** on any sqlite.org page and not a Hipp quote. (Apple's "many native apps" use is on famous.html, supporting it only indirectly.) Cut or attribute to the host.
  - **The Gingrich/Clinton budget-fight attribution** for the 2000 funding hiatus — Hipp's own memory-hedged recollection ("if I recall correctly"); Gingrich had left office by 2000. Use the **funding hiatus** as the load-bearing fact; treat the Gingrich/Clinton detail as a hedged aside or drop it.
  - **Motorola ~$80,000 first contract** — Hipp's own recollection ("I think it was $80,000"). Usable only as "by his own recollection."
  - **The "support the A350 for its 40-year airframe / through 2050" causal quote** — widely repeated but NOT extractable verbatim from the primary CoRecursive/Changelog transcripts. The independently verified facts are separate: (a) A350 uses SQLite, (b) the 2050 pledge exists. Do NOT script the 40-year-airframe → 2050 line as a direct quote.
  - **"Most thoroughly tested software" superlative** — does NOT appear verbatim on sqlite.org (the page says "Millions and millions of test cases"). Attribute to earned reputation, grounded in the 590x ratio + 100% MC/DC + four harnesses, not to a direct quote.
- **Hipp "more copies than people on earth"** — from Craig Stuntz's paraphrased notes of Hipp's **10 Oct 2017** talk (not 2020; not a verbatim transcript). Frame as "according to Stuntz's notes, Hipp said he thinks..."

## 9. Candidate cold-open hooks (hidden-dependency, verified facts only)

1. **The phone hook.** "Right now, on the phone in your pocket, there are hundreds of copies of the same little database — and across all the phones on earth, more than a *trillion* of them. You've never installed it. It has no server, no company, and it's in the public domain. It was written in the year 2000 by one man, for a US Navy warship." *(mostdeployed.html; CoRecursive)*
2. **The plane hook.** "The next time you fly an Airbus A350, the software keeping track of what needs fixing when you land runs on a database a single engineer wrote — and then gave away for free. The same database is in your browser, your phone, and the Library of Congress's list of formats meant to outlive us all." *(famous.html; locrsf.html — keep the A350 as maintenance-logging, per §8.)*
3. **The browser hook.** "Open a new tab and you're running it. Every Chrome, Firefox, and Safari ships the same database engine — one that competes not with Oracle, but with `fopen()`. It belongs to no one, because its author dedicated it to the public domain. And it started life as a damage-control program on a guided-missile destroyer." *(mostdeployed.html; whentouse.html; copyright.html; CoRecursive)*
